```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(behavSSF)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_ssf())
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev.args = list(bg = "white"))
```

Fitting estimates the model parameters. Decoding gives a state sequence and
state probabilities for each step. The ecological checks then assess whether
the fitted states meet the chosen rules. This vignette uses small, constructed
examples to show the calculations behind the workflow of
[Bouderbala, Nicosia and Fortin (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0360547).

## Exact small-model decoding

For two states and three steps there are only eight possible state paths.
The package's tests enumerate all eight to verify the likelihood, marginal
probabilities and most probable path independently of the recursion.

```{r decoding}
transition <- matrix(c(.8, .2, .35, .65), 2, byrow = TRUE)
emissions <- matrix(c(.2, .8, .9, .1, .3, .7), 3, byrow = TRUE)
decode_states(log(emissions), transition, initial = c(.4, .6))
```

Every independent segment restarts from its initial distribution. A gap in
observations must therefore create a new segment ID before fitting.

## An exactly checkable one-state fit

Each artificial stratum contains two alternatives with covariate values zero
and one. Value one is selected five times and value zero fifteen times. With
equal sampling weights and one control, the maximum is the binomial log odds
log(5/15). This provides a fitting check without relying on another optimizer.

```{r one-state}
n_steps <- 20L
chosen <- c(rep(1, 5), rep(0, 15))
data <- data.frame(ID = 1L, stratum = rep(seq_len(n_steps), each = 2),
                   obs = rep(c(1, 0), n_steps), w = 1,
                   x = as.vector(rbind(chosen, 1 - chosen)))
fit <- fit_ssf(data, ~ x, n_states = 1L, seed = 93)
print(fit)
c(estimate = coef(fit)[1, 1], reference = log(5 / 15))
fit$starts
```

## Movement signatures

The measure convention is required. For a kernel proportional to
exp(beta_step * r + beta_log_step * log(r)), the gamma shape is
beta_log_step + 2 under planar area and beta_log_step + 1 under step length
and angle. The sampling density must use the same measure. Annotate it with
`prepare_ssf_data(..., density_measure = "area")` or `"step_angle"`.
The guided workflow requires this metadata. `convert_density_measure()`
and `convert_movement_coefficients()` convert both parts consistently.

```{r metrics}
coefficients <- rbind(step = c(-1, -2, -3),
                      log_step = c(1, 0, -.5),
                      cos_angle = c(3, 1, .2))
movement_metrics(coefficients, convention = "area")
movement_metrics(coefficients, convention = "step_angle")
```

These summaries concern the intrinsic movement kernel. Habitat-dependent
selection can change the realised step-length distribution. The complete zebra generator uses a gamma step density divided by step length,
then multiplies it by the angular density. Its archived weights are therefore
area densities and are coherent with the article's +2 shape. No additional
Jacobian correction should be applied to them.

## Guided fitting on a new dataset

After preparing complete chronological case-control data, call
`fit_guided_ssf(data, convention = ...)`, optionally specifying a target
direction column. The assessment requires numerical convergence, a positive
Hessian, valid kernel summaries, occupancy support, transition bounds and
explicit movement ordering. It records why each rejected candidate failed.
The result may legitimately be `no_accepted_model`.

The HDT rule requires the entire unadjusted Wald interval for the target
coefficient to be positive. Smoothed probabilities describe the uncertainty
about individual states with the fitted parameters held fixed. Uncertainty
about the selected taxonomy would require a separate analysis.

## Combining angular effects

The intrinsic persistence coefficient and target coefficient jointly define
the conditional angular distribution. Its concentration depends on the target
bearing relative to the previous heading.

```{r angular}
angular_parameters(persistence = 2, target_bias = 1, relative_bearing = pi / 2)
```

## Numerical engines

`fit_ssf(..., engine = "native")` uses the compiled objective and analytic
gradient, including the derivative of the stationary initial distribution.
`engine = "R"` retains the independent R likelihood. The tests compare them
on independent segments, including singleton sequences and up to six states.
Rejected line-search trial points are counted in the numerical diagnostics;
no emission density is replaced to accept a final model.

## Controls and exact forward simulation

Here we generate independent lengths and angles for a small example. The
control sampler records the Jacobian used to express its density per unit area.

```{r controls-and-simulation}
set.seed(317)
n <- 80L
observed <- data.frame(ID = 1L, stratum = seq_len(n),
  step = rgamma(n, shape = 2, rate = 3), angle = runif(n, -pi, pi),
  previous_bearing = 0, target_bearing = 0)
proposal <- c(shape = 1, rate = 2, mean_angle = 0, concentration = 0)
choices <- generate_ssf_controls(observed, n_controls = 20L,
                                  proposal = proposal, seed = 318)
model <- fit_ssf(choices, n_states = 1L, seed = 319)
segments <- data.frame(ID = 1L, x = 0, y = 0, bearing = 0, n_steps = 100L)
simulations <- simulate_ssf(model, segments, n_sims = 10L, seed = 320)
movement_diagnostics(simulations$tracks[[1]], segments, lags = c(1, 2, 4))
```

The default simulator draws a fresh Markov state path. If you supply a fixed
decoded path, the simulation instead answers a conditional question about that
particular sequence. Both require correct segment starts. For POSIXct data sampled every
30 minutes, `prepare_ssf_data(..., time = "time", expected_interval = 1800)`
rejects gaps left inside an ID. The zebra sensitivity workflow also checks
step origins and retains short isolated sequences instead of joining them.

## Analytic normalisation and fitting without controls

For the canonical full-plane kernel, the radial integral is
Gamma(shape)/rate^shape. The angular integral is 2*pi*I0(kappa), where kappa
is the resultant concentration from persistence and any prospective target
direction. This is an exact integral for the supported kernel, without control
sampling. Extra endpoint habitat covariates, barriers and truncation do not
have this normaliser and are rejected.

```{r exact-fitting}
steps <- prepare_ssf_steps(observed, density_measure = "area")
exact_model <- fit_ssf(steps, n_states = 1L, normalization = "exact", seed = 321)
print(exact_model)
ssf_log_normalizer(coef(exact_model), convention = "area")
ssf_log_emissions(steps, ~ step + log_step + cos_angle,
  coef(exact_model), normalization = "exact")[1:4, , drop = FALSE]
exact_simulations <- simulate_ssf(exact_model, segments, n_sims = 10L, seed = 322)
movement_diagnostics(exact_simulations$tracks[[1]], segments, lags = c(1, 2, 4))
```

Target effects require `relative_target_bearing`, or `target_bearing` and
`previous_bearing`, selected at the start of each step. The endpoint cosine
alone is insufficient. Exact fits optimise log rate and log shape to enforce
positivity, then return coefficients, covariance and score on the natural scale.
The Hessian's working scale is identified separately. The tests check analytic
normalisers against independent quadrature and the compiled score against
finite differences of the R likelihood, including zero angular resultants.

Simulation bands from these examples describe repeated tracks at the fitted
parameters and the chosen model.


## Check the numerical fit in meaningful units

The raw gradient depends on the parameter units. Assessment uses the working
gradient divided by the square root of the corresponding observed-Hessian
diagonal. Its maximum must be at most 0.01. The native Hessian uses numerical differences of the analytic gradient.
Curvature is checked after dividing
each Hessian entry by the square root of the two diagonal entries. The smallest
eigenvalue must exceed 1e-8 times the larger of one and the largest eigenvalue.
These checks survive diagonal linear changes of parameter units. They do not
prove that the optimiser found the global maximum.

`fit$diagnostics$max_abs_scaled_gradient` reports the scaled score.
`fit$diagnostics$max_abs_gradient` retains the raw natural-scale score.
`fit$diagnostics$curvature` reports the scaled curvature. A small gradient with
weak curvature calls for closer inspection, rather than an ecological label.

## Declare a finite availability disk

For a canonical importance model, pass `step_max` when preparing the original
case and control rows. Use the same units as `step`:

```{r disk-support, eval=FALSE}
choices <- prepare_ssf_data(raw_choices, density_measure = "area", step_max = 3.8)
fit <- fit_ssf(choices, ~ step + log_step + cos_angle + canopy)
movement_metrics(coef(fit), "area", step_max = 3.8)
```

`assess_taxonomy()` and `summary()` read that support from the fit. A positive
linear distance coefficient can be integrable on this disk. The package checks
the behaviour near zero and uses the truncated radial mean for ordering. It
holds habitat covariates constant when computing that mean. This is not a
method for averaging movement over an arbitrary habitat polygon. Finite support
is currently unavailable with explicit step families or exact normalisation.

## Compare state coefficients within a rule

The rule receives labelled joint covariance as well as marginal standard errors.
For example, this additional rule asks whether the usual 95% Wald interval for
the persistence difference lies above zero:

```{r covariance-rule, eval=FALSE}
lengths <- ssf_taxonomy("lengths", c("Short", "Long"),
  rules = function(s) c(more_persistent =
    ssf_contrast(s, "cos_angle", from = "Short", to = "Long")$lower > 0))
```

The estimate is Long minus Short. Its variance includes the covariance between
the two fitted coefficients. A missing covariance gives a missing interval,
which fails the rule. This interval conditions on the fitted model. It does not
adjust for trying several taxonomies, state counts or solutions.
